prompt.context: A Ross MBA student is on a career trek to the exotic Caribbean island of Arborea Anna (AA). AA is not quite as rich or as technologically developed as the US. About 50% of the population has cell phones, and that percentage is increasing quickly. As the student wakes up, he looks out his hotel room window and sees a crew of workers from the AA Telephone Company ripping out the pay phone on the street corner and replacing it with a new model. He learns from the workers that they are not just installing a new model on this street corner, but replacing all 500 pay phones in the country with new models.
prompt.question: Why is the AA Telephone Company replacing all 500 pay phones with new models, given that pay phones are obviously a dying technology?

clarifying_info.q: What is different about the new model pay phone?
clarifying_info.a: The only significant difference is that the new model is equipped to accept payment via prepaid phone cards available at local convenience stores, in addition to traditional coin payment.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a competitor forcing this upgrade?
clarifying_info.a: Pay phone service in AA has been de-regulated, but no competitors to the privatized former government monopoly have entered the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a government mandate to update the technology?
clarifying_info.a: No, there is no government mandate to update pay phone technology.

clarifying_info.q: What is the useful life of a pay phone?
clarifying_info.a: Both the old and new model have a useful life of 10 years.

framework: Compare profitability of one old model phone versus one new model phone over useful life
Identify revenue drivers (customers per day, price per minute, advertising) and assess how each changes with new model
Identify cost drivers (installation, maintenance, interchange fees, rent) and assess how each changes with new model
Quantify cost differences to determine net savings per phone and total savings across all 500 phones

questions.prompt: How do revenue drivers change when switching to the new phone model?
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that revenue is essentially unchanged. The extra payment option (phone cards) may attract customers without coins, but this is offset by generally declining demand from cell phone growth. Price per minute is unaffected by supply/demand changes. Average call length may increase slightly but calls are priced with a flat fee for unlimited minutes so this does not affect revenue. There is no additional ad space on the new model.

questions.prompt: How do cost drivers change when switching to the new phone model?
questions.guidance: Installation cost is a significant one-time increase (new model must be purchased and installed). Maintenance cost is a significant ongoing decrease because the company won't have to empty coins from the machine as frequently — this is the KEY driver. Interchange fees may increase slightly as average call length increases, but this is insignificant. Rent is unchanged since land value is unaffected.

questions.prompt: Quantify the cost savings per phone and total savings across all 500 phones over the useful life of 10 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up old model total cost vs new model total cost over 10 years, then multiply the per-phone savings by 500. The key is recognizing that maintenance savings drive the decision. Assume discount rate of zero.

math.setup: Compare total cost (installation + maintenance over 10-year life) for old model vs new model per phone. Old model: no installation cost, $1,000/yr maintenance (based on $40/visit to unload quarters, 1 visit every 2 weeks, 50 weeks/yr = 25 visits x $40 = $1,000/yr). New model: $2,200 installation (equipment cost $2,000 + 10 hours labor at $20/hr = $200), $250/yr maintenance (1 visit every 8 weeks instead of every 2 weeks).
math.answer: Total cost savings of $2,650,000 across all 500 phones over 10 years

questions.prompt: What is the most important assumption made in your analysis, and how could you test it?
questions.guidance: The most important assumption is the reduction in the number of visits to empty quarters, driven by a significant number of consumers shifting to card payment. Without this behavioral shift, the maintenance savings do not materialize and the upgrade is not cost-justified. Testing methods: customer survey, benchmarks from other industries that have shifted to cashless payment, install one new phone and run a pilot.

questions.prompt: If you were the CEO of the AA Telephone Company, how would you spend the profits from these savings?
questions.guidance: Candidates should brainstorm strategic uses of profit. Strong answers include: pay dividends to shareholders, invest in new services (e.g., internet kiosks, mobile top-up services), pursue geographic expansion to other islands or markets.

brainstorming.prompt: If you were the CEO of the AA Telephone Company, how would you spend your profits?

categories.name: New Services
ideas: Offer mobile top-up services at pay phones

categories.name: Geographic Expansion
ideas: Enter other developing markets with similar pay phone infrastructure needs

recommendation: The AA Telephone Company is replacing its 500 pay phones to save maintenance costs
The new card-accepting model reduces the frequency of coin-collection visits from every 2 weeks to every 8 weeks, cutting maintenance cost from $1,000/yr to $250/yr per phone
Over the 10-year useful life, the new model generates $5,300 in net savings per phone, totaling $2,650,000 across the fleet
risks: The savings depend critically on consumers actually switching to card payment; if adoption is low, maintenance visit frequency will not decrease
Cell phone penetration is rising, which may reduce pay phone usage and revenue, though this does not affect the cost-saving logic
Installation must be executed efficiently to keep the $2,200 per-phone cost assumption valid
next_steps: Run a pilot with a small number of new phones to validate the assumed reduction in maintenance visits
Conduct a customer survey or benchmark cashless payment adoption from similar markets
Develop a rollout plan for all 500 phones that minimizes installation cost and disruption
